extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical researchers, and advanced graduate students
extracted.subtask_short: learning tools' limitations in math research
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for mathematical researchers on understanding, testing, and explaining the limitations of techniques and methods used in proofs and papers. Emphasises knowing counterexamples, obstructions, substitution options, and how to present limitations in expository/research writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate known vs unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: “An education isn’t how much you have committed to memory, or even how much you know. It’s being able to differentiate between what you do know and what you don’t.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the boundary between what you understand and what you do not; this self-knowledge is foundational to deciding which methods to try and avoiding wasted effort pursuing blind alleys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when your tools don't work
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mathematical education (and research papers) tends to focus, naturally enough, on techniques that work. But it is equally important to know when the tools you have don’t work, so that you don’t waste time on a strategy which is doomed from the start….”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying situations where a technique is doomed lets you stop wasting time and instead look for new tools or different problems; actively seek conditions or examples showing failure modes of your methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a library of counterexamples and model situations
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus, knowing a library of counterexamples, or easily analysed model situations, is very important….”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and study explicit counterexamples and simplified models to test methods, expose hidden assumptions, and clarify the exact scope of applicability of a tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand which obstructions a tool can or cannot resolve
rubrics_metrics.description: “…knowing the type of obstructions that your tool can deal with, and which ones it has no hope of resolving.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse the nature of obstructions (barriers) that arise in problems and map them to the strengths/weaknesses of particular techniques so you can predict success or failure in new situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know substitution circumstances and comparative advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: “Also it is worth knowing under what circumstances your tool of choice can be substituted by other methods, and what the comparative advantages and disadvantages of each approach is.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be fluent in alternative approaches; understand trade-offs (e.g., simplicity vs generality, shortness vs robustness) so you can pick or combine methods appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'magic wand' mentality
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you view one of your favorite tools as some sort of ‘magic wand’ which mysteriously solves problems for you, with no other way for you to obtain or comprehend the solution, this is a sign that you need to understand your tool (and its limitations) much better.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat tools as understandable techniques rather than black boxes; scepticism about mysterious successes prompts deeper study and prevents over-reliance on opaque methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test robustness by rewriting arguments without the tool
rubrics_metrics.description: “When this happens, you should try to see if there is a way to rewrite your argument in such a way that the tool is not used. If you understand your tool well, then you should be able to do this, though probably at the cost of making the argument significantly longer and messier. But if you do not see any way to proceed without the tool at all, then you should take this as a warning sign that you might not be using the tool properly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to reconstruct proofs without the specialised tool to check whether the tool is essential or is hiding gaps/implicit assumptions. Successful rewrites increase confidence; inability to rewrite suggests you need to analyse your usage of the tool more carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss known limitations of tools in papers
rubrics_metrics.description: “While unintuitive, one should also discuss the known limitations of a tool when writing a paper that uses that tool.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the tool's limitations in publications: this helps identify related problems suitable for the tool, enhances credibility and objectivity when comparing methods, signals where breakthroughs are needed, and prevents future readers from thinking limitations were overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conceal limitations (anticipate followups)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Finally, if one conceals the limitations of a tool from readers, and the work is interesting, eventually some followup work will run into the same limitations, and discuss them in their work; and it will appear that such issues were totally overlooked in your previous paper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiding limitations harms long-term perception of your work; frank discussion preempts criticism and situates your contribution accurately in the research landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the power of other mathematicians' tools and relearn the field
rubrics_metrics.description: See also: “learn the power of other mathematician’s tools” and “learn and relearn your field.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden your toolkit by studying others' methods and continually revisit core knowledge in your field to keep perspective on when different techniques are appropriate.
